entry.title: Combined summary - BIP draft: CISA for Taproot Key Path Spends
entry.summary: The recent discussions around the Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) draft have introduced a significant change in transaction signature handling through cross-input signature aggregation (CISA). This new methodology allows for Taproot-style key path spending, enabling inputs within a transaction to aggregate their signatures. Participants can choose from half-aggregation, full-aggregation, or opt out using a specific marker byte in their witness. Traditional script path spending remains unaffected, adhering to BIP 341/342 guidelines. For more information or to contribute feedback on this development, the draft text and a mock pull request are available for review [here](https://github.com/fjahr/bips/blob/cf0d4f2142cd0504b16e86739167b1f7ab9a3a06/bip-XXXX.mediawiki) and [here](https://github.com/fjahr/bips/pull/6). The technical evaluation of integrating Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) into existing BIP frameworks highlights several challenges, particularly with aggregated signatures and Elliptic Curve (EC) public keys in transaction outputs. The proposal suggests two potential solutions for EC public keys: tightly coupling CISA with P2TRv2 or obscuring them behind a hash in the ScriptPubKey. Both solutions aim to balance security and efficiency but come with trade-offs regarding quantum safety and transaction weight. The discussion underscores the complexity of adapting blockchain protocols to advanced cryptographic techniques while considering forward compatibility with emerging technologies like quantum computing. Additional insights from Fabian emphasize the need for new witness versions and output types to fully implement PQC mechanisms within the Bitcoin protocol. He acknowledges the data costs associated with hiding public keys for verification purposes, which could offset some benefits of aggregation. The conversation extends to strategic considerations for the network's readiness for Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs), highlighting the importance of consensus on the timeline and impact of PQ schemes. On the Bitcoin Development Mailing List, there has been an extensive debate about the feasibility of introducing multiple aggregation groups per transaction scheme. The idea was ultimately dismissed due to increased validation complexity without a justifiable use case. Discussions also proposed modifying the marker byte range in legacy scripts to distinguish between different aggregation methods, potentially impacting privacy by revealing participants in specific aggregation groups. These deliberations showcase the ongoing efforts to refine blockchain transaction processes, balancing implementation complexities against functional and privacy concerns.
